note: Subject pronouns are usually omitted in Italian (sono italiano); io is used for emphasis or contrast. Not capitalised.
Informal, for friends, family, young people; use Lei with strangers and in formal situations.
With a capital letter, Lei is the formal 'you' for one person (Lei è il signor Rossi?), used with the third-person verb form.
Plural of both tu and Lei in everyday speech.
Also the possessive 'their' (il loro libro, la loro casa), which never changes form.
Before most masculine singular nouns; lo before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, y; l' before a vowel. Plural: i.

en: the (masculine singular, before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, y)
note: lo studente, lo zio, lo gnocco; l' before a vowel (l'amico). Plural: gli. Also the object pronoun 'him/it'.
l' before a vowel (l'amica). Plural: le. Also the object pronoun 'her/it'.
Plural of il: il libro, i libri.

en: the (masculine plural, before vowel, s+consonant, z, gn, ps, y)
exEn: The students are in the classroom.
note: Plural of lo and of l' (masculine): l'amico, gli amici. Also the indirect object pronoun 'to him / to them'.
Plural of la and of l' (feminine): l'amica, le amiche. Also the pronoun 'to her'.
Also before vowels, with no apostrophe: un amico. Uno before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, y.

en: a; an (masculine, before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, y); one
note: uno studente, uno zio. Also the number one.
un' before a vowel: un'amica, un'idea.

ex: Il mio libro è sul tavolo.
exEn: My book is on the table.
note: Forms: mio, mia, miei, mie. Normally with the article (il mio), but no article with singular family members: mia madre, mio padre.
Forms: tuo, tua, tuoi, tue.
Forms: suo, sua, suoi, sue. Agrees with the thing owned, not the owner. Capital Suo = formal 'your'.
Forms: nostro, nostra, nostri, nostre.
Forms: vostro, vostra, vostri, vostre.
Forms: questo, questa, questi, queste; quest' before a vowel (quest'anno). Also a pronoun: Questo è mio.
Before a noun it follows the article pattern: quel libro, quello zaino, quell'amico, quella casa, quei libri, quegli amici, quelle case. As a pronoun: quello, quella, quelli, quelle.
a + article = al, allo, alla, all', ai, agli, alle. Used with cities (a Roma), times (alle otto) and 'a casa', 'a scuola'.
di + article = del, dello, della, dell', dei, degli, delle. 'Il libro di Marco' = Marco's book. Often d' before a vowel (d'accordo).
da + article = dal, dallo, dalla, dall', dai, dagli, dalle. 'Da Marco' = at Marco's place; 'dal medico' = at the doctor's.
in + article = nel, nello, nella, nell', nei, negli, nelle. Used with countries and regions (in Italia) and means of transport (in treno, in macchina).

exEn: I'm going to the cinema with Anna.
note: 'Con me', 'con te' (not 'con io'). Combined forms col / coi are optional.

exEn: I look for information on the internet.
note: su + article = sul, sullo, sulla, sull', sui, sugli, sulle: il libro è sul tavolo.
per + infinitive = in order to (studio per imparare). Also 'per Roma' = via / bound for Rome.

ex: Il bar è tra la banca e la posta.
exEn: The bar is between the bank and the post office.
note: 'Fra' means exactly the same. 'Tra un'ora' = in an hour (from now).
No accent (è with accent = is). 'Ed' is sometimes used before a vowel: ed è, ed anche.

exEn: Do you want tea or coffee?
note: 'Oppure' is a slightly stronger 'or else'.
'Però' is a common alternative.

ex: Perché studi l'italiano? Perché mi piace.
exEn: Why do you study Italian? Because I like it.
note: The same word is used in the question (why) and the answer (because). Accent on the final é.

exEn: When it rains, I stay at home.
note: Also a question word: Quando parti? = When are you leaving?

ex: Se hai tempo, vieni con me.
exEn: If you have time, come with me.
note: No accent (sé with accent = himself/herself). 'Non so se...' = I don't know whether...
Invariable. 'Di chi è?' = whose is it?; 'con chi?' = with whom?
In speech often shortened to 'cosa?' or 'che?': Cosa fai? Che fai?
Dov'è = where is; 'di dove sei?' = where are you from?
Com'è = how is / what is it like. Also 'like/as': bianco come la neve. 'Come ti chiami?' = What's your name?

exEn: How much does this book cost?
note: As an adjective it agrees: quanto, quanta, quanti, quante (Quanti anni hai?). 'Quant'è?' = how much is it?

ex: Qual è il tuo numero di telefono?
note: Forms: quale (singular), quali (plural). Before è it becomes qual, with no apostrophe: qual è.
The accent distinguishes it from si (reflexive/impersonal pronoun). 'Certo che sì' = of course.
At the end of a question it means 'right?': Vieni, no?
Goes before the verb (and before object pronouns): non lo so.
Often 'anch'io' (me too). Goes before the word it refers to, not at the end of the sentence.
Invariable as an adverb (molto bella, molto belli). As an adjective it agrees: molto, molta, molti, molte (molti amici, molta gente).

en: little; not much; few; not very
note: Adjective forms: poco, poca, pochi, poche (pochi soldi). 'Un po' (di)' = a bit (of).
più ... di = more than (più alto di me); il più = the most; 'non ... più' = no longer.
meno ... di = less than. Used in telling time: le otto meno dieci = ten to eight.
'Qua' is used the same way. 'Qui vicino' = near here.
'Là' is used the same way. The accent distinguishes lì from li (them).
From ci + è. Plural: ci sono. Negative: non c'è.

ex: Ci sono molti studenti in classe.
exEn: There are many students in the classroom.
note: Singular: c'è. Also 'I am there / I'm here': ci sono!

en: that; which; who (relative); what; how (in exclamations)
ex: La ragazza che vedi è mia sorella.
exEn: The girl (that) you see is my sister.
note: Invariable relative pronoun, never omitted in Italian. Also the conjunction 'that' (penso che...) and in exclamations: che bello!, che caldo!
Forms: tutto, tutta, tutti, tutte, followed by the article: tutta la classe, tutti i giorni. As a pronoun: tutto = everything, tutti = everyone.
Used for food, quality and good-hearted people. Before a masculine singular noun it becomes buon: buon giorno, buon appetito, un buon amico.
For taste, character and behaviour; for a bad situation or weather use brutto.
Before a noun it follows the article pattern: bel libro, bello zaino, bell'amico, bella casa, bei libri, begli amici, belle case.
Also for unpleasant things: una brutta notizia, un brutto voto.
'Di nuovo' = again.
For people 'anziano' is more polite. 'Un vecchio amico' = an old (long-standing) friend.
Same form for masculine and feminine. Also a noun: i giovani = young people.
Weather and feeling use other verbs: fa caldo = it's hot; ho caldo = I'm hot (not 'sono caldo').
fa freddo = it's cold (weather); ho freddo = I'm cold.
Same form for masculine and feminine. 'Facile da fare' = easy to do.
Same form for masculine and feminine.
Same form for masculine and feminine.

ex: Il negozio è aperto la domenica?
exEn: Is the shop open on Sundays?
note: Also 'open-minded' for people; 'all'aperto' = outdoors.
Sign on shops: Chiuso / Aperto.
pieno di = full of (pieno di gente). 'Il pieno, per favore' = fill it up (petrol).
Same form for masculine and feminine. Adverb: velocemente or 'veloce' colloquially.
Adverb: lentamente (slowly).
Same form for masculine and feminine. Also 'loud' (musica forte, parlare forte) and colloquially 'great, cool' (che forte!).
'Pronto?' is how Italians answer the phone (Hello?).
False friend: not 'brave' (coraggioso). Bravo! / Brava! / Bravi! = well done, agreeing with the person praised. 'Bravo a / in' = good at.
Opposite: sbagliato (wrong). 'Giusto!' = exactly, that's right.
Free = not busy or not taken (sono libero domani); free of charge is 'gratis' or 'gratuito'. Opposite: occupato.
'Vero?' at the end of a sentence = right?, isn't it? Opposite: falso.
Adverb (parlo bene l'italiano); the adjective is buono. 'Va bene' = okay; 'benissimo' = very well.
Also a noun: il male (pain, evil): mal di testa = headache. 'Non c'è male' = not bad.

ex: Bevo sempre un caffè la mattina.
exEn: I always have a coffee in the morning.
note: Usually placed after the verb. 'Per sempre' = forever.
Needs non before the verb: non ... mai. In questions = ever: Sei mai stato a Roma?
Invariable as an adverb; as an adjective it agrees: troppo, troppa, troppi, troppe (troppa gente, troppi soldi).

exEn: I like this city so much.
note: Adjective forms: tanto, tanta, tanti, tante (tanti auguri!). 'Tanto ... quanto' = as ... as.
Also 'like this': si fa così = you do it like this. 'Così così' = so-so.
As an adjective = alone (sono solo; solo, sola, soli, sole). 'Soltanto' = only; 'da solo' = by oneself.

en: oneself; himself; herself; themselves; each other; one (impersonal)
ex: Marco si lava le mani prima di mangiare.
exEn: Marco washes his hands before eating.
note: Reflexive and reciprocal pronoun of lui, lei and loro: si alza, si salutano. Also impersonal (qui si mangia bene = one eats well here) and passive (si vendono case). Becomes 'se' before lo/la/li/le/ne: se ne va. Not the same as sì (yes).
Short for 'che cosa'; the most common 'what' in spoken Italian, next to 'che'. Also the noun 'la cosa' = the thing.

ex: Il bagno è là, in fondo al corridoio.
exEn: The bathroom is over there, at the end of the corridor.
note: Same as 'lì' in everyday speech; 'là' points a little further or less precisely. The accent matters: la (the) vs là (there). 'Di là' = over there / in the other room; 'qua e là' = here and there.
Plural of 'tutto' used as a pronoun: tutti (masculine or mixed), tutte (feminine). Before a noun it takes the article: tutti i giorni, tutte le sere. 'Tutti e due' = both.
